name: Pedro Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Pedro. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. I'm going to describe five pictures of how AI might change work and ask how you'd react. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, go ahead. I'm Pedro, 43. I drove lorries for twenty years, long distance, and last year I switched to carpentry. So I'm the new boy on site, with grey in my beard.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Before the pictures, tell me about a normal working day for you. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We're rebuilding the main railway station, a huge job, three or four years. I'm on temporary works, so the timber hoardings round the site, stair towers, walkways for the public, and fitting out the site cabins. Before work I ask the AI on my phone to explain whatever I got wrong yesterday, like how to brace a hoarding against wind. I like being home every night after twenty years of sleeping in a cab, and I like that you can see what you did. What wears me out is being slow, and the older carpenters calling me 'the driver'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, the market's spoken, it was a tool not a miracle. I'd say it online too, I'm on a couple of drivers' forums still. Nobody should be crying about it, just get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine either way. I've got two rental houses, Ana's got her salon, and I've got a trade I'm learning. I left the lorries because I saw a truck drive itself on a test track. If that turns out to be hype, well, I lost a truck and got my own bed back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Learn the trade, use the AI to get faster, finish my ticket in about two years. Keep the houses let and maybe buy a third when the price is right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like I made a good move whichever way it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you saw a truck drive itself. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was 2025, at a depot, they were testing one. It went round the yard and reversed onto a loading bay better than half the lads I know. I went home and told Ana I had five years at most, and I started looking that week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use the AI in carpentry, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I take a photo of the drawing and ask it what I'm looking at. I ask it to quiz me on the stuff for my exams while I'm on the train home. Last week I asked it why my stair stringer was out, and it was right, I'd measured from the wrong edge.

S0.say: I'd say the market has spoken and AI was a tool, not a miracle. I'd say it on drivers' forums too, and tell people to get on rather than cry about it.
S0.think: He'd be fine either way, with two rental houses, his wife's salon and a trade to learn. Even if self-driving trucks were hype, he now sleeps at home.
S0.do: Keeps learning carpentry with AI help and aims to finish his ticket in about two years. Keeps the houses let and considers buying a third when prices suit.
S0.feel: Calm, sure he made a good move either way.
S0.quote: If that turns out to be hype, well, I lost a truck and got my own bed back.
S0.fieldNote: Pedro got out of trucking early after watching a self-driving lorry in 2025. He uses AI daily to learn the trade, like a pocket tutor. Property and his wife's salon give him a strong base and a confident, free-market tone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is normal, every generation gets its shake-up, and you move or you get left. I'd say people shouldn't wait for the government to save them. Get a skill, get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. I'm already the one on site using AI to learn, so I'd pick up the new tools faster than the old hands. The older carpenters call me the driver now, but in this picture they'd be asking the driver how the new kit works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the site to put me on whatever new machines come in, straight away. I'd use the AI to help Ana run the salon bookings and stock, which would free her up. I might buy a third rental with some of the savings, because people still need somewhere to live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a bit pleased with myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My old driving mates, some of them. Big Joe's 58 and won't touch a smartphone. I'd tell him what I told myself, move now while you choose, not later when they choose for you. He'd tell me where to go, nicely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people shouldn't wait for the government. Would you accept any help from it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For training, fine, that's a hand up. But I don't want my taxes paying people to sit at home. My father worked until his back gave out and never took a penny, and that's how I was raised.

S1.say: I'd say every generation gets a shake-up and you either move or get left. People shouldn't wait for government to save them; get a skill and get on with it.
S1.think: He thinks it's good for him because he already uses AI to learn and would pick up new tools faster than the older hands.
S1.do: Asks to work with any new machines on site straight away and uses AI to help run his wife's salon bookings and stock. May buy a third rental house with savings.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit pleased with himself.
S1.quote: The older carpenters call me the driver now, but in this picture they'd be asking the driver how the new kit works.
S1.fieldNote: Pedro sees steady disruption as his chance to flip the 'new boy' label. His traditional values show in accepting training help but not handouts, rooted in his father's example. His advice to an older driving friend is to move while he still gets to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough, but the people who move fastest will come through. I'd say don't sit and wait for a cheque, find where the work's going. I'd probably say it a bit harder than I should on the forums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it worries me a little, but not because of carpentry. If AI and robots take every job in two years, then my tenants lose their jobs too, and then who pays the rent? I thought owning houses was the safe bit. In this picture the houses are only as safe as the people renting them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd move fast into whatever job runs or checks the robots on site, even if it's a pay cut at first. I'd sell one of the rental houses while prices are still good and put part of the money into shares in the companies making the robots. Ana and I would look at a small robot or AI system for her salon, to cut costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit tight in the chest, but I've jumped before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What would you be doing in those two years while you see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Moving, constantly. Selling one house, buying shares, getting myself onto the robot side of the job. Two years is short, but I left trucking with about the same, and it worked. You don't get a second warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell a house. Isn't that just betting on the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. But I'd rather own a piece of the thing that's winning than hold on to something that's losing value. It's what I did with trucking, I didn't wait for the company to decide for me.

S2.say: I'd say it'll be rough but the fastest movers will come through, so don't wait for a cheque; find where the work is going. He'd say it harder than he should on forums.
S2.think: He worries a little, but about his rental houses rather than carpentry: if tenants lose their jobs, rent stops. The houses are only as safe as the people renting them.
S2.do: Moves straight into a job running or checking robots on site, even at a pay cut. Sells one rental house while prices hold, puts part of the money into robot company shares, and looks at a robot or AI system for his wife's salon.
S2.feel: Uneasy and tight in the chest, but confident from jumping before.
S2.quote: I thought owning houses was the safe bit. In this picture the houses are only as safe as the people renting them.
S2.fieldNote: Pedro's worry in the fast picture is surprising: not his job but his tenants' ability to pay. He'd sell a house and buy into robot companies, repeating his trucking move. Having acted fast once, two years feels workable to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you start now. Learn the new tools, sort your money, don't wait for someone to tell you. I'd say it to anyone at church who looked worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is good for me. I'd finish my ticket, then move onto the robot side of site work, and I'd know both. I'd be the carpenter who understands robots, and the robot man who knows what a straight wall looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd finish my exams and ask the station contractor about their robot plans, and get my name down. I'd use the AI to learn robot programming basics in the evenings. I'd keep both houses for now and slowly put some savings into shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, which I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change for you, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't have to sell a house in a hurry. I can learn properly instead of grabbing. And my tenants get time to adjust too, which keeps the rent coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mateo and Clara?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo's twelve, he's mad about engines, like me. I'd tell him learn to fix robots, because something always breaks. Clara's nine and wants to do hair like her mum, and I'd say good, people will always want a person touching their hair.

S3.say: I'd say five years is plenty if you start now: learn the tools, sort your money and don't wait to be told.
S3.think: He thinks five years suits him: he'd finish his ticket and move onto robots, knowing both carpentry and machines.
S3.do: Finishes his exams in year one, asks the station contractor about robot plans and puts his name down. Learns robot programming basics with AI in the evenings, keeps both houses and slowly buys shares.
S3.feel: Calm and busy, which he likes.
S3.quote: I'd be the carpenter who understands robots, and the robot man who knows what a straight wall looks like.
S3.fieldNote: Five years removes Pedro's need to sell property in a hurry and gives his tenants time too. He wants to be the carpenter who understands robots. His hopes for his children are practical: fix robots, or do hair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so no excuses. I'd say families should plan, young people should learn useful trades, and nobody should expect the government to carry them. I'd say it nicely, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is easy for me. I'd get properly good at carpentry, then move onto the machines, and maybe start my own small firm with a couple of robots. I've spent half my life behind a wheel watching other people build things. I'd like ten years of building before the robots get their turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the ticket, work a few years, then around year five buy a small robot and start a business doing hoardings and site cabins for contractors. Keep the houses, keep investing. Put money aside for Mateo and Clara's training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Looking forward to it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Starting a business with robots. Doesn't that put other carpenters out of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, some. But if I don't, someone else will, and I'd rather it was a local man who hires local lads to work beside the machines. Somebody's going to own the robots, so it might as well be a lorry driver from round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the decade that you'd dread?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching some of my driving mates go under because they waited. I'd try to drag them along, but you can't make a man move. And maybe the day the station's finished, because I'll miss that job.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift with no excuses: families should plan, young people should learn useful trades, and nobody should expect government to carry them.
S4.think: He thinks ten years is easy for him: master carpentry, then machines, then perhaps his own firm with robots. He wants ten years of building after half a life behind a wheel.
S4.do: Finishes his ticket, works a few years, then around year five buys a small robot and starts a business doing hoardings and site cabins. Keeps the houses, keeps investing and saves for his children's training.
S4.feel: Calm and looking forward to it.
S4.quote: Somebody's going to own the robots, so it might as well be a lorry driver from round here.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Pedro plans to become a small business owner running robots and hiring local people beside them. He accepts that this may displace other carpenters, reasoning someone will own the robots anyway. His only dread is friends who waited too long.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, but only because of the tenants and my mates, not me. What would help is cheap training for people who want to move, and fewer rules stopping small men like me from buying the machines and starting up. Families and churches can do the rest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Ana. She's the real reason I could jump, because her salon kept us steady while I learned. People talk about who's brave enough to change, but usually there's someone at home holding the floor.

headlineQuote: I've spent half my life behind a wheel watching other people build things. I'd like ten years of building before the robots get their turn.
portrait: Pedro Baker is a 43-year-old junior carpenter on temporary works at a big railway station rebuild, who drove lorries for twenty years and left after seeing a self-driving truck in 2025. He owns two rental houses, his wife Ana runs a hair salon, and he uses AI every day as a pocket tutor. He's traditional and free-market, wants hand-ups not handouts, and believes in moving before you're pushed. He stays calm in most pictures, only uneasy at AGI in two years because his tenants might stop paying, and with more time he plans to become a carpenter who runs robots and later owns a small firm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because of his tenants and his old driving mates rather than himself.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap training for people who want to move, and fewer rules stopping small operators from buying machines and starting up.
